new_statements.quote: 2.3.7 STRESS. Tindal stress is almost always penultimate, but occurs word-finally in some words with final heavy syllables. Emphasis seems to cause stress to become word-final. This is problematic for my data, because many of the forms have been elicited in isolation, and words in isolation are often emphasized. Word-final stress appears to be permitted only on heavy syllables, but not all such syllables take final stress. Example (62) illustrates instances of penultimate stress, whereas (63) shows final stress. [fn. 2, p. 2:] In this paper, stress has only been indicated if it is not penultimate.
new_statements.citation: Robinson, Laura C. 2005. A Sketch Grammar of Tindal Dusun. University of Hawai'i at Manoa Working Papers in Linguistics 36(5): 1-33.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 2.3.7 'Stress', printed p. 9 (PDF p. 11); also fn. 2 p. 2 and sec. 2.3.6 pp. 8-9
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (33 pp., text layer, ScholarSpace hdl 10125/73202 = UHWPL 36(5), open access; metadata re-confirmed online). extracted text of PDF p. 11 (header '9') contains exactly: '2.3.7 STRESS. Tindal stress is almost always penultimate, but occurs word-finally in some words with final heavy syllables. Emphasis seems to cause stress to become word-final. This is problematic for my data, because many of the forms have been elicited in isolation, and words in isolation are often emphasized. Word-final stress appears to be permitted only on heavy syllables, but not all such syllables take final stress. Example (62) illustrates instances of penultimate stress, whereas (63) shows final stress.' follow…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable by default; a minority of words with a heavy (closed or long/diphthongal) final syllable carry final stress instead, and emphatic/citation pronunciation tends to shift stress to the final syllable. The author also attributes the prepenultimate /a/ > /o/ neutralization to stress being 'nearly always penultimate' (sec. 2.3.6).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress on some words with heavy final syllables (examples 63: tanayon, tompios, gipan, walay, dula, lapap, marked with acute accent in the original); not all heavy finals take it; emphasis (words elicited in isolation) seems to move stress to the final syllable. Loanwords discussed separately (sec. 2.4) without stress comment.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based largely on forms elicited in isolation from one speaker; author explicitly warns that isolation/emphasis may induce final stress, so citation-form vs. phrase-medial behaviour is not separated.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Tindal Dusun of Kota Belud (speaker from Kelawat district), i.e. Tempasuk Dusun, which Glottolog 5.1 lists as dialect temp1235 of Kadazan Dusun cent2100 (former ISO [tdu], merged into [dtp] by ISO 639-3 CR 2015-060). Robinson calls it 'a coastal dialect of Central Dusunic'. It is not a description of the standard Bundu-Liwan (Central Dusun) or Penampang Coastal Kadazan (coas1294) varieties; the primary phonology for those, Miller 1993, could not be opened. Based on one consultant, elicitation through English; the working-paper series asks readers to note its preliminary nature.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3.7 (p. 9): Tindal stress is almost always penultimate; word-final in some words with final heavy syllables; emphasis (e.g. citation forms) seems to shift stress to the final syllable; final stress only on heavy syllables but not all heavy finals take it.
